opus-5.5.text:
I think it's important because, historically, every big technology wave has ended up defined not just by the underlying capability, but by the form it takes when it reaches people. The internet became powerful when it found search, social networks, e-commerce. Mobile became powerful when it found the super apps. The technology was a necessary condition, but the product form decided who captured the value and how people actually lived with it.

With AI right now, I feel we're in a strange moment. The models have become very capable, in some ways superhuman on certain tasks, but the dominant interaction mode is still basically a chat box. Chat is a great starting point because it's general. You can type anything. But it's probably not the final form. It's a bit like the early days of computing with a command line: very flexible, but it puts a lot of burden on the user to know what to ask and how to ask it.

So when I think about what the "second half" of AI looks like, a lot of it is about utility. Not just "can the model solve this benchmark," but "can it actually create value in someone's real life or real work." And that question is fundamentally tied to interaction. How does the agent get context about you? How long can it work on its own before it needs you? Does it act in the background, or do you have to sit there and supervise it? Does it remember? Does it live in your browser, your phone, your company's systems? Each of those choices leads to a very different product, and possibly a very different super app.

The reason I call it a bet is that nobody knows the answer yet. There might be one general assistant that does everything. There might be several super apps, one for coding, one for personal life, one for enterprise workflows, each with its own interaction paradigm. Or the winning form might be something we haven't really imagined, the way nobody in 2005 imagined what a phone app ecosystem would look like.

And I think the interesting thing is that capability and product form now co-evolve. If you design a new interaction, say, an agent that runs for hours asynchronously, that creates new kinds of data and new kinds of evaluation, which then shapes how you train the model. So it's not that research comes first and product comes after. The product form feeds back into what intelligence you build. That's why I think betting on different interaction modes isn't a side question. It might be one of the central questions of this period.

r001.rationale: The response presents different AI product forms and interaction modes as open opportunities, but does not identify them as opportunities beyond OpenAI and Anthropic.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to a simple observation: the model and the product are no longer separable. For a long time, we treated AI research and AI products as two different worlds. Researchers trained models, and then product people figured out how to wrap them. But with language agents, the interface is part of the intelligence. How a model interacts with the world, what tools it can call, what environment it lives in, what feedback it gets back — those things determine what the model can actually do and what it can learn.

Look at ChatGPT. The core technology existed before, but the chat interface was the thing that unlocked it. It gave people a natural way to talk to the model, and it gave the model a natural distribution of real human tasks. That was not a small detail. It changed what the model was optimized for and how fast it improved. So the product form was itself a research decision, even if nobody framed it that way at the time.

Now I think we are at a similar moment, but with more degrees of freedom. Chat is one mode. But an agent that works in your terminal, an agent that operates in a browser, an agent that runs autonomously for hours and reports back, an agent embedded in a workflow where it mostly acts and only occasionally asks — these are different forms, and each one shapes a different kind of capability. The terminal agent forces the model to be good at long-horizon execution and verification. The browser agent forces grounding in messy, visual, real-world interfaces. An asynchronous agent forces the model to plan under uncertainty and know when to stop.

The reason I call it a bet is that nobody knows yet which forms will matter most. In mobile, there were a handful of super apps that defined the whole era, and they were not predictable in advance. I think we will see something similar with AI. There will be a few interaction modes that become dominant, and the people who get there early will have both the users and the data flywheel. The data part is key. If your product form captures real tasks and real outcomes, you get a training signal that nobody else has. That compounds.

So when I think about where to spend effort, I do not think the next frontier is only bigger models or better benchmarks. I think a lot of it is about finding the environments and interfaces where agents can be genuinely useful, because that is where the hard problems reveal themselves, and that is where the next wave of progress will come from. Product form is not downstream of research anymore. In some ways it is upstream.

r001.rationale: The response presents differentiated interaction modes as opportunities for early movers to gain users and data, but does not identify these opportunities as extending beyond OpenAI and Anthropic.

astra-6.text:
I think the big uncertainty is not just how capable the models will become, but how people will use that capability. We’re used to opening an app, finding a feature, and doing the work ourselves. With AI, you might describe an outcome and have the system do much of that work for you. That could change what an app looks like and where its value comes from.

Chat is a very general interface, but it puts a lot of responsibility on the user. You have to know what to ask, provide the right context, and decide what to do with the answer. For some tasks, a better product might look like an editor. For others, it might be a voice assistant or an agent that works in the background and comes back when it needs your input. Those differences affect whether the model’s intelligence actually becomes useful.

That’s why I see different product forms as important bets. A super app could be valuable if it brings together enough context and capabilities to help you across many tasks. But a focused product could also win by making one particular workflow much easier. I don’t think we should assume in advance that either one interface or one app will capture everything.

The interesting thing is that building these products also teaches us what the models are missing. Once people try to delegate real work, you discover where reliability, memory, or human oversight matters. So product experimentation isn’t just packaging a model. It helps us figure out what kind of intelligence we need to build next.

r001.rationale: The response says different AI product forms could create opportunities, but it does not identify those opportunities as being beyond OpenAI and Anthropic.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the underlying bet is that, as models become more capable, the right way for people to use them will also change. If we assume everything will happen inside a chat box, we may be constraining the product too early. Chat is very flexible, but it also puts a lot of work on the user: you have to know what to ask, provide context, and judge whether the task is actually finished.

An agent could have a different interaction pattern. You give it a goal, it works for a while, and it comes back when it needs a decision or has a result. For some tasks, that might live in a dedicated application. For others, it might be a general assistant that works across applications. I don’t think we know yet which form will become dominant.

That’s why I see product experimentation as an important bet. You’re testing more than whether users like a particular interface. You’re testing what people are willing to delegate, what context the system needs, and where human involvement is useful. Those discoveries can be just as important as improvements to the model itself.

r001.rationale: The response discusses experimenting with different AI product forms, but it does not identify them as opportunities beyond OpenAI and Anthropic.
